traits: Uniform pale yellow-green color across the whole lawn, most visible on older, lower blades
Growth slows and the lawn thins evenly with no distinct pattern
No lesions, pustules or pattern of spots on the blade

copy.what_it_means: A uniform pale yellow-green lawn, worse on older blades, can suggest low nitrogen, but early disease or a root problem can look similar. A photo cannot confirm it; a technician checks the pattern and times any nutrition within the local fertilizer rules.
copy.fact: Florida's sandy soils hold nitrogen poorly, so it can wash below the root zone with heavy rain well before a lawn shows visible signs of running low.

tech_notes: Rule out rust and disease first; nitrogen timing is restricted by the local fertilizer blackout (Jun 1 - Sep 30) for nitrogen and phosphorus.

differentials.difference: Nitrogen deficiency is a uniform pale color on older blades; iron deficiency stripes the newest blades with green veins and yellow tissue between them.

differentials.difference: Nitrogen deficiency has no pustules; rust shows orange, powdery pustules on the blade that rub off on a finger.
differentials.next_observation: A close-up of your fingertip after rubbing a blade: orange powder that rubs off points to rust.

condition.recovery_note: Color often improves within two to three weeks once nutrition is corrected.

traits: Interveinal yellowing on the newest blades, giving a striped look while the veins stay green
Leaves can turn nearly white in severe cases while older blades stay green
Most common in spring after new growth outpaces the roots' ability to take up iron

copy.what_it_means: Yellow-striped new blades with green veins can suggest low iron, most common in spring, but a photo cannot rule out a disease. A technician checks the pattern and times any nutrition within the local fertilizer rules.
copy.fact: Iron is usually present in Florida soil; the shortage is more often about roots being too immature in spring to take it up fast enough.

tech_notes: Common after spring nitrogen applications outpace root uptake capacity on bahiagrass, centipedegrass and St. Augustinegrass.

traits: Blotchy, interveinal yellowing on older blades, sometimes with a reddish tinge along the margins
Turf looks pale or 'hungry' even when mowing and watering are adequate
Most visible on older, lower leaves rather than new growth

copy.what_it_means: Blotchy, interveinal yellowing on older blades, sometimes with a reddish tinge at the margins, can suggest low magnesium, but a photo cannot rule out other causes. A technician checks the pattern and times any nutrition within the local fertilizer rules.
copy.fact: Magnesium leaches easily from Florida's sandy soils, and research has found the response to added magnesium varies a lot by region and soil type.

tech_notes: Response to added magnesium is inconsistent between regions; confirm soil test values before recommending it as the primary fix.

traits: Translucent yellow-orange spotting or marginal and tip necrosis confined to the oldest fronds
Affected older leaflets can look withered and frizzled while newer fronds stay normal
Symptoms progress in stages from translucent spotting to necrotic tips to whole leaflet death as the deficiency deepens

copy.what_it_means: Translucent spotting or necrotic, frizzled leaflet tips confined to the oldest fronds can suggest low potassium, but early lethal bronzing looks the same. A technician asks about early fruit drop or blackened flower stalks and checks the pattern before timing nutrition within local rules.
copy.fact: Because potassium moves within the plant, a palm short on it pulls potassium out of its oldest fronds first to support new growth, which is why symptoms always start on the oldest leaves.

tech_notes: Confirm symptoms are confined to oldest fronds only (newer fronds normal) to separate from lethal bronzing, which progresses upward through the whole canopy; ask about early fruit drop or blackened flower stalks. This is the single most common nutrient problem in Florida landscape palms.

symptoms: Translucent yellow-orange spotting or marginal and tip necrosis confined to the oldest fronds
Affected older leaflets can look withered and frizzled while newer fronds stay normal

required_signature.text: A close-up of the oldest fronds showing translucent spotting or necrotic, frizzled leaflet tips, while newer fronds stay normal.

differentials.difference: Potassium deficiency and early lethal bronzing can look identical on the oldest fronds alone; only the pattern over time and a lab test tell them apart.
differentials.next_observation: Ask about early fruit drop or blackened flower stalks; a repeat wide canopy photo in 2-3 weeks checks for upward movement, then a lab test confirms.

differentials.difference: Potassium deficiency shows spotting or necrosis on the oldest fronds; magnesium deficiency bands the oldest fronds' margins with a green center.
differentials.next_observation: A close-up of an affected frond checking for spotting versus a margin band.

differentials.difference: Potassium deficiency develops gradually and stays on the oldest fronds; cold damage appears within days of a cold snap and can affect many fronds at once.
differentials.next_observation: A technician checks how many fronds are affected and whether the damage lines up with a recent cold snap.

condition.recovery_note: Existing damaged leaflets do not recover, but new fronds emerge healthier over several months once nutrition is corrected.

traits: Broad yellow bands along the margins of the oldest fronds with the center staying green
Symptoms appear only on the oldest fronds; newer growth stays normal
Common where sandy soil has leached out magnesium over time

copy.what_it_means: A broad yellow band on the margins of the oldest fronds, with the center staying green, suggests low magnesium. It does not rule out other causes; a technician checks the pattern before timing any nutrition within the local rules.
copy.fact: When a palm is short on both magnesium and potassium at once, the oldest fronds show the potassium pattern while magnesium symptoms show up on the middle fronds instead.

tech_notes: Best prevented in containers with dolomite amendment; in the landscape, confirm the band is confined to oldest fronds before recommending nutrition.

differentials.next_observation: A wider photo of the whole canopy checking how far the discoloration has spread.

differentials.difference: Magnesium deficiency bands the margin with a green center on the oldest fronds; potassium deficiency shows spotting or necrosis on the oldest fronds instead.
differentials.next_observation: A close-up of an affected frond checking for a margin band versus spotting.

condition.recovery_note: New fronds emerge healthier over several months once nutrition is corrected; older affected fronds do not recover.

traits: Newest emerging leaves are yellow with streaky, dead lines running along their length
New leaflets look withered, curled and 'frizzled', worst near the base of the leaf
Common on palms grown in alkaline, high-pH soil

copy.what_it_means: Streaky yellow, withered, 'frizzled' new leaves suggest low manganese, common in alkaline soil. It can be serious for pygmy date palms in particular; a technician checks the soil and the newest growth before timing any nutrition within the local rules.
copy.fact: This is sometimes called frizzle top because the newest leaflets curl inward around the leaf's central rib, giving the whole young leaf a frizzled look.

tech_notes: Common in pygmy date palms on alkaline soil; unlike potassium deficiency, this starts on the newest leaves, not the oldest.

differentials.difference: Manganese deficiency frizzles and streaks the newest whole leaf; boron deficiency shows hooked leaflet tips or a spear leaf that fails to fully open.

differentials.difference: Manganese deficiency streaks and withers the newest leaf's leaflets; iron deficiency yellows the newest leaves between the veins without withering them.
differentials.next_observation: A close-up of the newest leaf checking for withered streaking versus even interveinal yellowing.

condition.recovery_note: New fronds emerge healthier within a few months once nutrition is corrected; already frizzled leaves do not recover.

traits: Newest spear leaf fails to open fully, or emerges with sharply bent, hooked leaflet tips

Symptoms are limited to the newest growth; older fronds stay normal

copy.what_it_means: Hooked leaflet tips or a spear leaf that will not fully open suggest low boron. A technician checks whether the spear leaf is failing to open versus something more serious, then times any nutrition within the local rules.
copy.fact: A palm can be temporarily short on boron just from heavy rain leaching it from the soil, even when the soil normally has enough.

tech_notes: Symptoms are confined to newest growth; distinguish a spear leaf that fails to open from one that pulls free easily (bud rot).

differentials.difference: Boron deficiency keeps the spear leaf attached even if it will not open; bud rot leaves discolor, wilt and pull free easily from the crown.
differentials.next_observation: A technician checks whether the spear leaf pulls free; don't climb a ladder to reach it yourself.

traits: Interveinal or uniform yellowing on the newest leaves while older leaves stay green
New leaflets may show necrotic tips and stunted growth in severe cases
Usually tied to poor soil aeration or planting depth rather than a lack of iron in the soil

copy.what_it_means: Yellowing newest leaves, while older leaves stay green, suggest low iron. This is usually about the roots and drainage rather than a lack of iron in the soil; a technician checks planting depth and drainage before timing any nutrition within the local rules.
copy.fact: Iron deficiency in palms is usually not a shortage of iron in the soil at all; wet, low-oxygen roots simply cannot take up the iron that is already there.

tech_notes: Check for deep planting or waterlogged soil around the root zone before assuming a soil nutrient shortage.

traits: Yellow new leaves with the veins staying green
Older leaves stay green while the newest growth looks pale
Worse near slabs, walkways and limestone or alkaline soil

copy.what_it_means: Yellow new leaves with green veins on shrubs such as ixora or gardenia suggest a micronutrient problem, often tied to alkaline soil rather than a pest. A technician checks the soil conditions and the site before timing any nutrition within the local rules.
copy.fact: This kind of yellowing is often about soil pH: in alkaline or limestone-influenced soil, the iron and manganese are present but the plant cannot take them up.

tech_notes: Not a pest. Check for alkaline soil, limestone fill or slabs near the root zone, and drainage. Interveinal chlorosis on new growth points to iron or manganese; confirm before assuming which.
